CARVEYANCE

Feature Carveyance

Scale Model Warfare

Two tiny cars. Seventy years of rivalry, ruin, reinvention, and revenge — and the strange twist at the end where the winner ends up owning the loser. The full story of Matchbox versus Hot Wheels.

Feature · 1:64 Scale, Life-Size Grudge · Die-Cast & Dynasty

Photo — Hero, full width

The two combatants, side by side. A vintage Lesney-era Matchbox (in its little box, muted realistic livery) next to a Redline-era Hot Wheels (flame card, candy paint, red-stripe tires) — same surface, raking light, so the reader feels the whole philosophical split in one frame: humble realism versus chromed desire. A collector's flat-lay works beautifully here.

There is a specific weight a die-cast car has when you pick it up off the carpet. Heavier than it looks. Cold at first, then warm from your hand. A little door that opens if you're lucky, wheels that spin if you flick them, a scratch on the roof from the time it went off the edge of the coffee table. Most of us owned dozens of these things and threw most of them away without a thought. What we didn't know, kneeling on the living room floor with a fistful of them, is that we were holding the front line of one of the longest-running rivalries in the history of consumer products — a decades-long grudge match between a scrappy English workshop and an American toy juggernaut that would end in bankruptcy, exile, revenge, and one of the more delicious corporate ironies of the 20th century.

This is the story of Matchbox and Hot Wheels. Who came first, who hit harder, why they feel so different in your hand, and how they ended up, improbably, living under the same roof. It starts, as the best origin stories do, with a little girl, a rule about spiders, and a road roller.

Part One · London, 1953

A Man Named Odell, and a Box of Matches

To understand Matchbox you have to understand Jack Odell, and to understand Jack Odell you have to accept that the man was, by any reasonable measure, not supposed to end up a millionaire.

John William "Jack" Odell was born in East London in March 1920, into a working-class family with no cushion under it. He was expelled from his council school at thirteen. At fourteen he went to work for Simms Motor Units, and for the next several years he took whatever jobs kept him fed — driving a van, running errands at an estate agent's, threading film through a cinema projector. He was, in the classic British mold, a self-taught mechanical mind: someone who understood metal and machines not from a lecture hall but from taking things apart and building them again until they worked.

After the war, Odell fell in with two men who happened to share a surname despite being unrelated — Leslie Smith and Rodney Smith. In 1947 the three of them formed a small die-casting company in London, and named it with a mashup of the founders': Leslie plus Rodney equals Lesney. Odell's name didn't make the cut — a small indignity that will rhyme with a bigger one later, on the American side of this story. Lesney Products didn't set out to make toys. It made industrial die-castings, the kind of unglamorous small metal parts that go into other people's products: automotive dashboard fittings, door handles. Toys were a sideline, something to keep the machines busy when the industrial orders went slack.

Then came the moment that built an empire — and like all good origin stories, it exists in two competing versions.

The tidy version, the one you'll read on museum placards: Odell's young daughter Anne attended a school with a rule that children could only bring toys small enough to fit inside a matchbox. Wanting his daughter to have something to show off, Odell took one of Lesney's existing toy castings — a green-and-red road roller — and shrank it down until it fit in a matchbox. The messier, more human version, which the Odell family has also told: Anne kept coming home with spiders and creepy-crawlies stuffed inside matchboxes, to her father's exasperation, and Odell struck a deal — if she stopped bringing home bugs, he'd make her a toy that fit inside the box instead. Either way, the result was the same: a tiny, exquisitely made metal roller, packaged in a replica matchbox, that stopped other parents in their tracks. Where do I get one of those?

The Matchbox name arrived in 1953, and the first cars followed close behind. The original 1-75 range — so called because it eventually ran from number 1 to number 75 — launched with a small fleet that included that road roller, a dumper truck, a cement mixer, and a Massey Harris tractor. They were cheap on purpose. Odell and the Smiths understood something profound about children: a toy a kid can buy with their own pocket money, with coins they scrounged themselves, hits differently than a toy a parent buys for them. Matchbox cars cost pennies. A child could walk into a shop, alone, feeling enormous, and walk out an owner.

It worked at a scale that's hard to overstate. By 1960 Lesney had gone public, and Odell — the East London kid expelled at thirteen — had made his first million before turning forty. "I made it with a few days to spare," he liked to say. By the mid-1960s Lesney was moving on the order of a hundred million toys a year, and American children alone were buying Matchbox cars by the tens of millions annually. In 1956 the company had even launched a second line, Models of Yesteryear — beautifully detailed replicas of vintage vehicles, aimed not at kids at all but at adult collectors. This was a genuinely radical idea in the 1950s: a toy company deliberately making toys for grown-ups. Matchbox didn't just build a product. It quietly invented the die-cast collector — a fact that will matter enormously by the end of this story.

For fifteen years, in the small-car business, Matchbox simply was the business.

Photo — medium

The one that started it all. The original Lesney road roller, ideally beside a real matchbox for scale, so readers see the actual object the whole empire grew from. The Strong National Museum of Play holds strong reference imagery of early Matchbox pieces.

Part Two · California, 1968

The Ambush

Mattel was not a car company. Mattel was a Barbie company.

The firm had been founded in a Los Angeles garage in 1945 by a trio: Harold "Matt" Matson and the married couple Ruth and Elliot Handler. The name, like Lesney's, was a portmanteau of its founders — Matt plus Elliot — which means Ruth Handler, arguably the most consequential of the three, got left out of the company's name entirely. (Years later her own husband explained why with a shrug: they just couldn't make "Ruth" fit. She got her revenge by inventing Barbie in 1959 and turning Mattel into a giant.) Matson sold out early due to poor health, leaving the Handlers in charge, and through the 1950s and '60s Mattel rode dolls and novelty toys to the top tier of the American toy industry.

But Elliot Handler kept looking at the little cars — specifically, the little cars his company didn't make, the ones from England and from Corgi that American kids were snapping up. Handler had an instinct, and a competitive itch, and a simple, aggressive question: what if we made one of those, except better? Not more realistic. Not more accurate. Faster. Cooler. Meaner-looking. What if we built a miniature car for the kid who didn't want a scale model of his dad's sedan, but a chopped, slammed, candy-colored hot rod that looked like it was doing ninety while sitting still?

To get there, Mattel did something a British die-caster would never have thought to do: it hired a car guy. Harry Bentley Bradley was a real automotive designer, fresh from General Motors, who'd worked on genuine full-size custom and concept cars. Bradley didn't approach the assignment like a toymaker shrinking a real car down to fit a package. He approached it like a customizer — raking the stance, fattening the wheel wells, exaggerating every line that made a car look fast. Eleven of the first sixteen Hot Wheels castings came off his board.

Those first sixteen have a nickname among collectors that has stuck for over half a century: the Sweet 16. Hot Wheels made its debut at the 1968 New York Toy Fair, and the line officially went on sale on May 18, 1968 — a date Mattel still marks as the brand's birthday. The roster read like a hot-rodder's fever dream: the Custom Camaro (the first one sold), the Custom Mustang, Custom Corvette, Custom Barracuda, Custom Firebird, Custom Cougar, Custom T-Bird, Custom Eldorado, Custom Fleetside, Custom Volkswagen, the Deora, the Ford J-Car, the Hot Heap, the Silhouette, the Python, and the Beatnik Bandit.

That last one tells you everything about Hot Wheels' DNA. The Beatnik Bandit wasn't a model of a production car — it was a miniature of a genuine, wild custom built by the legendary hot-rod artist Ed "Big Daddy" Roth, a fiberglass bubble-topped dream machine with a clear plexiglass dome that Roth had shaped by softening a sheet of plastic in a giant pizza oven. Mattel called Ed Roth and asked permission to shrink it. Where Matchbox looked at the street and made faithful copies of what was on it, Hot Wheels looked at car culture's outer fringe — the show cars, the customs, the impossible dream machines — and made those.

Matchbox modeled reality. Hot Wheels modeled desire.

But the sculpting wasn't even the killer feature. The killer feature was underneath. Every other die-cast car on the market, Matchbox included, rolled on relatively thick metal axles that dragged with friction. Mattel's engineers did something clever: they ran thin, hardened-steel piano-wire axles through low-friction plastic bearings, then added a styling touch that became the brand's signature — a red stripe painted around each tire. The result was a car that, set down at the top of a slope, would take off. It rolled farther, faster, and freer than anything a kid had ever felt. Mattel leaned all the way in, selling bright orange plastic track with loops and jumps that turned a living room floor into a gravity-powered speedway. A Matchbox car placed next to a Hot Wheels car at the top of that track didn't just lose. It looked, humiliatingly, like it was parked.

The effect on the market was instant and brutal. Mattel's little cars, in the words of one account, set the toy market on fire. American sales of Matchbox — the brand that had owned this category for fifteen years — cratered. Corgi reeled. In a single season, an English institution went from undisputed king of the small-car world to a company scrambling to understand what had just hit it. What had hit it was a red-striped tire and a piece of piano wire.

Photo — full width

Orange track, and the reason it mattered. The iconic Hot Wheels orange track with a loop, ideally mid-action with a car in the curve. This is the single object that won the war — worth showing in its full gravity-powered glory.

Part Three · 1969

The Empire Strikes Back (Slightly Too Late)

Here is a detail that Lesney's engineers must have found simultaneously infuriating and liberating: Mattel never patented the low-friction wheel.

That oversight handed the Brits a lifeline, and they grabbed it. By 1969 — barely a year after the ambush — Lesney had re-engineered its entire range around a new low-friction wheel system it called Superfast. Thinner axles, sharper-edged free-spinning wheels; the models could finally roll with something approaching Hot Wheels pace. Lesney even reworked its paint, ditching some of its trademark restraint for the brighter, wilder colors Mattel had proven kids wanted. The story goes that Lesney was so unsure how fast it could get the new wheels working that it printed its 1969 catalog with all the old slow-wheel models, then scrambled the Superfast versions out mid-year once the factory sorted it out.

Superfast closed the gap. It did not close the story. And this is the crucial, poignant thing about the whole rivalry: after 1968, Matchbox was almost always responding. It had spent fifteen years setting the terms of the small-car world, and it spent the next several decades reacting to terms set in California. The company that invented the category was now playing catch-up in it.

The Fall

Death by a Thousand Cuts (One of Them Red-Striped)

For a while, catch-up was enough — Lesney was still a huge company, still selling toys by the hundred million, still employing thousands in London. But the 1970s came for it from several directions at once. Children's attention was fragmenting: Star Wars toys arrived and vacuumed up shelf space and pocket money; the first video games began to glow in arcades and living rooms. A small metal car now had to compete not just with a faster small metal car, but with a lightsaber and a joystick. Lesney's attempts to diversify beyond die-cast mostly missed. Its overreliance on the core Matchbox line — once its greatest strength — became a fatal exposure. And the broader British economy of the era, all inflation and industrial strife and a strong pound that made English exports expensive abroad, pressed down on a company whose whole model depended on being cheap.

By 1980 the strain was structural. Lesney announced it would cut roughly a sixth of its workforce of about 7,500. Jack Odell, by then retired, came out of retirement in 1981 as joint vice-chairman to try to save the thing he'd built. It wasn't enough. In the summer of 1982, Lesney Products went bankrupt. The company that had started with a road roller in a matchbox, that had made an East London dropout a millionaire before forty, that had put a little metal car in the fist of nearly every child in the Western world — collapsed into receivership. And the single biggest reason, threaded through all the others, was the red-striped tire that had rolled out of a California garage fourteen years earlier.

Part Four · 1982–1997

Exile, Wandering, and an Ironic Homecoming

What happened to Matchbox next is a corporate odyssey with more owners than a used Matchbox car has at a swap meet.

When Lesney fell in 1982, the brand didn't die — it got sold off. On September 24, 1982, a Hong Kong–based toy entrepreneur named David Yeh, who ran a firm called Universal Toys, bought the Matchbox name, tooling, moulds, and assets out of receivership. Yeh moved production to Far East factories and relaunched the operation as Matchbox International Ltd. Matchbox was now, for the first time, not a London company at all.

Jack Odell, meanwhile, did the most Jack Odell thing imaginable. Rather than ride off, the seventy-something engineer bought up much of Lesney's old tooling and machinery himself and started a brand-new die-cast company to make the detailed, larger-scale historical models he loved. He named it by spelling his own name backwards: Lledo. The man who'd been left out of "Lesney" put himself front and center this time, and kept making tiny beautiful metal things nearly until his death in 2007.

Matchbox itself kept changing hands. In 1992, the American toy company Tyco Toys — then the third-largest toymaker in the United States — bought Matchbox from Universal. And that acquisition set up the final, delicious twist. In November 1996, Mattel announced it would buy Tyco Toys outright. The deal — around $755 million — cleared federal regulators and closed in March 1997. It handed Mattel something like a fifth of the entire U.S. toy market, and it handed Mattel, almost incidentally, the crown jewel buried inside Tyco's catalog: Matchbox.

Sit with that for a second. The brand that Hot Wheels had ambushed in 1968. The brand whose American sales Hot Wheels had gutted. The brand that had gone bankrupt in no small part because of Hot Wheels, then wandered through Hong Kong and New Jersey for fifteen years — came home in 1997 to live inside the very company that had knocked it down. Mattel now owned both the disruptor and the disrupted. The winner had bought the loser. The most famous rivalry in the history of toy cars became, on paper, a rivalry between two brands with the same parent.

And here's the genuinely smart part: Mattel didn't fold Matchbox into Hot Wheels or quietly kill it. It kept both alive and pushed them to opposite corners. Hot Wheels would keep doing what it had always done best — fantasy, speed, customs, spectacle — while Matchbox would be repositioned as its mirror image: the realistic one, the brand of everyday cars and working trucks and things you actually see on the street. The two toys that had spent thirty years trying to destroy each other were now, deliberately, designed not to compete. Reality in one hand, fantasy in the other.

The Whole War, On One Line

Seventy Years, Eight Turning Points

1947
Lesney is founded in London — an industrial die-caster, not a toymaker.
1953
The Matchbox name debuts; the 1-75 range begins with a road roller.
1956
Models of Yesteryear launches — a toy line aimed at adults. The die-cast collector is born.
1968
Hot Wheels arrives with the Sweet 16 and low-friction wheels. Matchbox's US sales crater.
1969
Matchbox counters with Superfast, closing the speed gap — but now it's the one reacting.
1982
Lesney goes bankrupt. The brand is sold to Universal Toys of Hong Kong.
1997
Mattel buys Tyco — and with it, Matchbox. The winner now owns the loser.
2026
Both brands hit Hollywood: a Matchbox movie lands in October, a Hot Wheels film in development.

Part Five · In the Hand

Why They Feel So Different (It's Not Your Imagination)

Pick up a Matchbox car and a Hot Wheels car and you can feel the philosophies fighting, even now.

The scale tells the first story. Both brands live at roughly 1:64 — about two and a half to three inches long — but neither is religious about it, and they break the rules in opposite directions. Matchbox tries to keep a vehicle's proportions honest, so a fire truck looks like a fire truck and a delivery van has a van's dimensions. Hot Wheels cheerfully distorts: it'll drop a roofline, widen a stance, and balloon the wheel arches until the car looks like it's straining against physics — accuracy sacrificed on the altar of cool. A Matchbox car wants you to recognize it. A Hot Wheels car wants you to want it.

The wheels tell the second story, and it's the same story as 1968. Hot Wheels was born from a performance breakthrough and never let go of it; the whole brand is organized around the sensation of speed — orange track, loops, the car that rolls forever. Matchbox's Superfast wheels were a defensive reaction, a way to stop the bleeding, and the brand's soul was never really about velocity. It was about the little details: the door that opens, the dump bed that tips, the crane that swings.

The subject matter tells the third. Matchbox is a catalog of working life — sedans, ambulances, cement mixers, tow trucks, buses, bulldozers, the machinery of an actual functioning town. Its play pattern is building a world: laying out a construction site, staging an emergency, running a city on the rug. Hot Wheels is a catalog of dreams — muscle cars, supercars, chopped customs, movie tie-ins, and vehicles that never existed and never could. Its play pattern is spectacle: how fast, how high, how far, how big a loop.

You can even read the difference in the packaging. Matchbox literally came in a little box, humble and utilitarian, right down to the name. Hot Wheels came blister-packed on a flame-branded card that looked like an advertisement for adrenaline. One brand whispered here is a nice little truck. The other shouted here is the fastest thing you have ever owned.

Matchbox

The realist · "What is the world made of?"

  • Honest proportions, true to life
  • Working features — doors, beds, cranes
  • Everyday cars, trucks, working machines
  • Play pattern: build a functioning world
  • Humble cardboard box
  • Invented the adult collector, 1956

Hot Wheels

The dreamer · "What if it were faster?"

  • Exaggerated stance, dropped rooflines
  • Built around speed and the orange track
  • Customs, supercars, the impossible
  • Play pattern: spectacle — how high, how fast
  • Flame-branded blister card
  • Instant scarcity by constant new castings

Neither is better. They're answers to different questions. Matchbox answers what is the world made of? Hot Wheels answers what if the world were faster and cooler and a little bit insane?

Part Six · The Underworld

Where the Cars Get Expensive

Here is where the two-and-a-half-inch car stops being a toy and starts being an asset class.

Because Matchbox invented the adult collector back in 1956, and because Hot Wheels created instant scarcity with constant new castings and color variations, both brands sit atop deep, obsessive, sometimes eye-wateringly expensive secondary markets. The vintage sweet spots are well defined: for Hot Wheels it's the Redline era (1968–1977), named for that signature red-striped tire; for Matchbox it's the early Lesney-made pieces from the brand's London heyday.

And then there's the holy grail — a car so rare it has become the stuff of legend. In 1969, Hot Wheels designed a Volkswagen bus called the Beach Bomb, modeled on the classic Microbus, with two little surfboards meant to load through the back window. Two problems: the prototype was too narrow to roll properly on the track, and the rear-loading surfboards looked awkward. Mattel redesigned it for mass production, widening the body and moving the surfboards to the sides. Which means the original rear-loading prototypes — especially a couple made in pink, a color Mattel produced in tiny numbers on the theory that boys wouldn't want it — became almost mythologically scarce. Only two pink rear-loading Beach Bombs are known to exist. One belongs to collector Bruce Pascal, whose Hot Wheels holdings run to thousands of pieces worth around $2 million collectively, and that single little pink bus has been valued at roughly $150,000.

A hundred and fifty thousand dollars. For a toy car. That was rejected before it ever went on sale.

It is, by a wide margin, the most valuable Hot Wheels on Earth — a monument to the strange truth that the things nobody wanted at the time become the things everybody wants later. And note the poetry of it: the crown jewel of the fantasy brand is a miniature of a Volkswagen bus, one of the most gloriously un-fantastical vehicles ever built. Even Hot Wheels' most valuable dream started as a working van.

Part Seven · The Scoreboard

Who's Winning Now? (It's Not Close, But It's Not Over)

If the 1968 ambush decided the war, the decades since have decided the peace, and the peace belongs to Hot Wheels.

The numbers are staggering. Mattel produces more than 500 million Hot Wheels cars a year — about sixteen and a half every single second — and has made something north of 8 billion of them since 1968. To put that in perspective, the entire global automotive industry builds somewhere around 80 to 90 million real cars in a year. Mattel makes more Hot Wheels in twelve months than every automaker on the planet combined has built real cars in the last several years. There is a decent chance Hot Wheels is the single most-manufactured "vehicle" in human history.

Sources: Mattel · OICA global production figures

And it's still growing. Hot Wheels posted worldwide gross sales of roughly $1.43 billion in 2023, $1.58 billion in 2024, and about $1.75 billion in 2025 — with Mattel citing 2024 as its seventh consecutive record year for the brand. Mattel now talks about Hot Wheels the way it talks about Barbie: as a "power brand," a franchise, a cultural platform rather than a product.

The franchise now sprawls the way Barbie's does: a Netflix animated series, Hot Wheels Let's Race, running since 2024; a renewed partnership with the NHRA drag-racing world; touring Monster Trucks events; the annual Legends Tour, where fans' real customized cars get turned into official castings; the members-only Red Line Club for serious collectors; tech-chipped id cars; and a live-action Hollywood movie in development at Warner Bros. with J.J. Abrams' Bad Robot producing and Wicked director Jon M. Chu attached to direct. There are also those Guinness World Records that keep the brand's daredevil promise literal: a toy-scale loop-the-loop measured at 12 feet 8 inches; a life-size double-loop stunt pulled off by professional drivers pulling seven G's; a 332-foot record ramp jump in a full-size truck.

Matchbox, by comparison, is the quieter sibling — and tellingly, it no longer even gets its own line in Mattel's earnings reports, folded instead into the broader "Vehicles" category dominated by its old rival. But quiet isn't the same as struggling. Matchbox has carved out a genuine identity as Mattel's grown-up, conscientious brand — the company's sustainability standard-bearer. In 2022 it released the first-ever CarbonNeutral-certified Matchbox die-cast, a Tesla Roadster made from 99% recycled materials, as a blueprint for a brand-wide goal of using 100% recycled, recyclable, or bio-based materials by 2030. It has partnered with EV makers, leaned into electric vehicles and charging-station playsets, and doubled down on the realism and detail that always set it apart.

And it's about to get its own moment in the sun. Matchbox: The Movie, an action-adventure starring John Cena, is set to premiere globally on Apple TV on October 9, 2026 — directed by Sam Hargrave, the stunt-specialist behind the Extraction films, from Skydance Media and Mattel Films, with a cast that includes Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Teyonah Parris, Arturo Castro, and Danai Gurira. It arrives, appropriately, right around the time the Hot Wheels film is taking shape — the two toys chasing Hollywood the same way they've chased each other since Nixon was in office.

So the scoreboard reads clearly: Hot Wheels is bigger, richer, louder, faster, and more culturally omnipresent, and has been for decades. But Matchbox is very much alive, occupying the one piece of ground Hot Wheels never wanted — the honest, everyday, buildable, recyclable real world — and doing it as the respected elder of the whole category, the brand that started it all.

Coda

The Thing in Your Hand

Here's what makes this rivalry worth caring about, beyond the numbers and the acquisitions and the $150,000 pink bus.

Two little cars, born fifteen years and five thousand miles apart, turned out to embody two completely different theories of what a toy is for. One says a toy should show you the world as it is — the roller, the fire truck, the working van — and let your imagination furnish the rest. The other says a toy should show you the world as it could be if it were louder and faster and had a flame job, and let your imagination floor it. Matchbox is the world you live in. Hot Wheels is the world you dream about at eight years old with your cheek against the carpet, watching a candy-colored blur take a loop at what feels, in that moment, like the speed of light.

The astonishing part is that both bets paid off — that both little cars are still here after seventy-plus years, and that in the end the same company holds them both: the disruptor and the disrupted, reality and fantasy, sitting in the same box, waiting for the same small hand to reach in and decide, today, which kind of world it wants.

Most of us threw them away. A few of us should probably go check the attic.
